blocks.p: Now when the captains saw the answer of the great ones, and that they could get no hearing from the old natives of the town, and that Mansoul was resolved to give the King’s army battle, they prepared to meet them and to try it out by strength of arm. First they made their force more formidable against Ear-gate, for they knew that unless they could break through there, nothing could be done against the town. That done, they put the rest of their men in their places and gave out the watchword, which was, “You must be born again.” [John 3:7] Then they sounded the trumpet, and those in the town answered them, shout for shout and charge for charge, and so the battle began. Now the townspeople had planted two great guns on the tower over Ear-gate, one called High-and-mighty and the other Headstrong. They trusted much in these two guns, which had been cast in the castle by Diabolus’s gunfounder, Mr. Puff-up; and mischievous pieces they were. But the captains, once they saw them, were so vigilant and watchful that although the shot would sometimes whiz past their ears, it did them no harm. The townsfolk never doubted that with these they would sorely harass the camp of Shaddai and keep the gate secure; but they had little cause to boast of the damage they did, as what follows will show.
Famous Mansoul also had some smaller pieces, which they used against the camp of Shaddai.

Those in the camp fought just as stoutly, and with what may truly be called valor they let fly as fast at the town and at Ear-gate; for they saw that unless they could break open Ear-gate, it would be useless to batter the wall. Now the King’s captains had brought several slings with them, and two or three battering rams. With their slings they battered the houses and people of the town, and with their rams they tried to break Ear-gate open.

The camp and the town had several skirmishes and sharp encounters, while the captains with their siege engines made many brave attempts to break open or beat down the tower over Ear-gate and to force their way in at the gate itself. But Mansoul held out so stubbornly, through the rage of Diabolus, the valor of the Lord Willbewill, and the leadership of old Incredulity the Mayor and Mr. Forget-Good the new Recorder, that the cost and labor of that summer’s war on the King’s side seemed almost entirely lost, and the advantage seemed to be swinging back to Mansoul. But when the captains saw how things stood, they made an orderly retreat and dug themselves into their winter quarters. Now in this war, as you may well imagine, there was much loss on both sides, of which please accept the following brief account.

When the King’s captains marched from the court to come against Mansoul, they happened, as they crossed the country, on three young fellows who had a mind to become soldiers: fine men they were, and to all appearances men of courage and skill. Their names were Mr. Tradition, Mr. Human-Wisdom, and Mr. Man’s-Invention. They came up to the captains and offered their service to Shaddai. The captains told them what they were about and warned them not to be rash in their offer; but the young men said they had thought it over already, and had come on purpose to meet the captains and enlist under them. So Captain Boanerges, because they were men of courage, enlisted them in his company, and away they went to the war.

Now once the war had begun, in one of the sharpest skirmishes, a company of the Lord Willbewill’s men sallied out at the sally port, the postern gate of the town, and fell on the rear of Captain Boanerges’s men, where these three fellows happened to be. They took them prisoner and carried them into the town, and before long the streets were full of talk of the three notable prisoners the Lord Willbewill’s men had brought in from the camp of Shaddai. At length word reached Diabolus in the castle of what my Lord Willbewill’s men had done, and whom they had taken.

Then Diabolus called for Willbewill to learn the truth of the matter. He asked, and Willbewill told him. Then the giant sent for the prisoners, and when they came, he demanded who they were, where they came from, and what they had been doing in the camp of Shaddai; and they told him. Then he sent them back to their cell. A few days later he sent for them again and asked whether they would be willing to serve him against their former captains. They told him that they did not live so much by religion as by the turns of fortune, and that since his lordship was willing to take them on, they were willing to serve him. Now while this was going on, there was in the town of Mansoul one Captain Any-side, a man who made himself very busy there; and to this Captain Any-side Diabolus sent these men, with a note in his own hand telling him to receive them into his company. The letter read as follows:
Any-side, my darling,

The three men who bring you this letter wish to serve me in the war, and I know of no one better to put them under than you. Receive them, therefore, in my name, and as need requires, make use of them against Shaddai and his men. Farewell.
So they came, and he received them. Two of them he made sergeants, but Mr. Man’s-Invention he made his ensign, the bearer of his colors. But enough of this; now to return to the camp.

Those in the camp did some damage to the town as well. They beat down the roof of the Lord Mayor’s house, and so left him more exposed than he had been before. With a sling they very nearly killed my Lord Willbewill outright, though he managed to recover. But they made a notable slaughter among the aldermen, for with a single shot they cut down six of them: Mr. Swearing, Mr. Whoring, Mr. Fury, Mr. Stand-to-Lies, Mr. Drunkenness, and Mr. Cheating.

They also knocked the two guns off the tower over Ear-gate and laid them flat in the dirt. I told you before that the King’s noble captains had drawn off to their winter quarters and dug in there with their baggage and gear, so that, to the best advantage of their King and the greatest annoyance of the enemy, they might give the town of Mansoul timely and hot alarms. And this plan hit its mark so well that I may say they did almost what they pleased to harass the town. For now Mansoul could not sleep securely as before, nor go to its debauchery as quietly as in times past; for they had from the camp of Shaddai such frequent, hot, and terrifying alarms, yes, alarm upon alarm, first at one gate and then at another, and then at all the gates at once, that their former peace was broken. Indeed, the alarms came so often, and that when the nights were longest, the weather coldest, and the season therefore most unseasonable, that that winter was to the town of Mansoul a winter all its own. Sometimes the trumpets would sound, and sometimes the slings would whirl stones into the town. Sometimes ten thousand of the King’s soldiers would be running around the walls of Mansoul at midnight, shouting and raising the cry for battle. Sometimes, again, some in the town would be wounded, and their cries and lamenting would be heard, to the great distress of the now languishing town. Yes, they were so hard pressed by their besiegers that, I dare say, Diabolus their king had his rest badly broken in those days.

In those days, as I was told, new thoughts, and thoughts that ran against one another, began to take hold of the minds of the men of Mansoul. Some would say, “There’s no living like this.” Others would reply, “This will soon be over.” Then a third would stand up and answer, “Let’s turn to King Shaddai, and so put an end to these troubles.” And a fourth would come in with a fear: “I doubt he’ll take us back.” The old gentleman, too, the Recorder who had held that office before Diabolus took Mansoul, began to talk aloud, and his words were now to the town of Mansoul like great claps of thunder. No noise was so terrible to Mansoul now as his, together with the noise of the soldiers and the shouts of the captains.

Things also began to grow scarce in Mansoul; the things her soul had craved were now departing from her. A blight lay on all her pleasant things, and burning instead of beauty. Wrinkles now, and some marks of the shadow of death, were on the people of Mansoul. And now, oh, how glad Mansoul would have been to enjoy quietness and contentment of mind, even joined with the poorest condition in the world!

In the depth of that winter the captains also sent, by the mouth of Boanerges’s trumpeter, a summons to Mansoul to surrender herself to the King, the great King Shaddai. They sent it once, and twice, and three times, thinking that at some point there might be in Mansoul some willingness to surrender, if only they had the cover of an invitation to do it under. Indeed, as far as I could gather, the town would have surrendered to them before now, had it not been for the opposition of old Incredulity and the fickleness of my Lord Willbewill’s thoughts. Diabolus also began to rave. So Mansoul was not yet of one mind about yielding, and they still lay distressed under these perplexing fears.
I told you just now that the King’s army sent to Mansoul three times that winter, calling on her to submit.

The first time the trumpeter went, he went with words of peace. He told them that the captains, the noble captains of Shaddai, pitied and grieved over the misery of the now perishing town of Mansoul, and were troubled to see them stand so much in the way of their own deliverance. He said, moreover, that if poor Mansoul would now humble herself and turn, her former rebellions and most notorious treasons would be forgiven by their merciful King, yes, and forgotten too. And having warned them not to stand in their own way, nor set themselves against themselves, nor make themselves their own losers, he went back to the camp.

The second time the trumpeter went, he dealt with them a little more roughly. After the trumpet sounded, he told them that their continuing in rebellion only chafed and heated the spirit of the captains, and that the captains were resolved either to conquer Mansoul or to lay their bones before the town walls.

He went again the third time and dealt with them more roughly still. He told them that now, since they had been so horribly profane, he did not know, did not certainly know, whether the captains were inclined to mercy or to judgment. “Only,” he said, “they commanded me to summon you to open your gates to them.” So he returned and went into the camp.

These three summonses, and especially the last two, so distressed the town that they at once called a consultation, and the result was this: that my Lord Willbewill should go up to Ear-gate and there, with a sound of the trumpet, call to the captains of the camp for a parley. So the Lord Willbewill sounded from the wall, and the captains came up in their armor, with their ten thousands at their feet. Then the townsmen told the captains that they had heard and considered their summons, and would come to an agreement with them and with their King Shaddai on certain terms, articles, and proposals which they had been appointed, by order of their prince, to put forward. On these grounds, they said, they would agree to be one people with them:

1. That those of their own party, namely the present Lord Mayor and their Mr. Forget-Good, together with the brave Lord Willbewill, might remain, under Shaddai, the governors of the town, the castle, and the gates of Mansoul.
2. That no man who now served under their great giant Diabolus should be turned out by Shaddai from house, harbor, or the freedom he had enjoyed until now in the famous town of Mansoul.

3. That the town of Mansoul should be granted the enjoyment of certain of its rights and privileges: namely, those formerly granted it, which it had long enjoyed under the reign of its king Diabolus, who now was, and long had been, its only lord and great defender.
4. That no new law, officer, or executor of law or office should have any power over them without their own choice and consent.
“These are our proposals, our conditions of peace,” they said, “and on these terms we will submit to your King.”
But when the captains heard this weak and feeble offer from the town of Mansoul, and its high and bold demands, they answered them through their noble captain, Captain Boanerges, with this speech:

“O inhabitants of the town of Mansoul, when I heard your trumpet sound for a parley with us, I can truly say I was glad. When you said you were willing to submit yourselves to our King and Lord, I was gladder still. But when, by your silly provisos and foolish quibbles, you laid the stumbling block of your iniquity before your own faces, my gladness was turned into sorrow, and my hopes of your return, so well begun, into faint and failing fears.

“I take it that old Mr. Dwell-on-it, the ancient enemy of Mansoul, drew up these proposals that you now present to us as terms of agreement; but they do not deserve to be allowed to sound in the ear of any man who claims to serve Shaddai. We therefore jointly, and with the highest disdain, refuse and reject such things as the greatest of iniquities.

“But, O Mansoul, if you will give yourselves into our hands, or rather into the hands of our King, and will trust him to make such terms with you and for you as seem good in his eyes (and I dare say you will find them the most profitable to you), then we will receive you and be at peace with you. But if you do not care to trust yourselves in the arms of Shaddai our King, then things are just where they were before, and we know what we have to do.”

Then old Incredulity, the Lord Mayor, cried out: “And who, being out of their enemies’ hands, as you see we are now, would be so foolish as to take the staff out of their own hands and put it into the hands of they know not whom? For my part, I will never yield to so unlimited a proposal. Do we know the manner and temper of their King? Some say he will be angry with his subjects if they happen to step a hair’s breadth out of the way; and others, that he requires of them far more than they can perform. So it seems, O Mansoul, that your wisdom is to take good heed what you do in this matter. For once you yield, you give yourselves up to another, and then you are no longer your own. To give yourselves up to an unlimited power is the greatest folly in the world; for then you may indeed repent, but you can never justly complain. And do you even know, once you are his, which of you he will kill and which of you he will save alive? Or whether he will not cut off every one of us, and send out of his own country a new people and settle them in this town?”

This speech of the Lord Mayor undid everything and threw their hopes of an agreement flat to the ground. So the captains returned to their trenches, to their tents, and to their men, as they were; and the Mayor went to the castle and to his king.

Now Diabolus had been waiting for his return, for he had heard that the two sides had been at it over terms. So when the Mayor came into the chamber of state, Diabolus greeted him: “Welcome, my lord. How did matters go between you today?” Then the Lord Incredulity, with a low bow, told him the whole of it: “Thus and thus said the captains of Shaddai, and thus and thus said I.” Diabolus was very glad to hear it, and said, “My Lord Mayor, my faithful Incredulity, I have tested your loyalty more than ten times already, and never yet found you false. I promise you, if we get through this crisis, I will promote you to a place of honor, a place far better than Lord Mayor of Mansoul. I will make you my deputy over everything, and next to me you shall have all nations under your hand. Yes, and you shall put bonds on them so that they cannot resist you; nor shall any of our subjects walk at liberty any more, except those who are content to walk in your fetters.”

So the Lord Mayor came away from Diabolus as if he had truly won a favor. He went home in great state, and thought to feed himself well enough on hopes until the time came for his greatness to be enlarged.

But though the Lord Mayor and Diabolus agreed so well, this rebuff to the brave captains threw Mansoul into mutiny. For while old Incredulity went into the castle to congratulate his lord on what had passed, my Lord Understanding, who had been Lord Mayor before Diabolus came to the town, and the old Recorder, Mr. Conscience, got word of what had happened at Ear-gate. (You must know that they had been kept away from that debate, for fear they would mutiny there on the captains’ side.) They were much troubled by what they heard. So they gathered some of the townspeople together and began to impress on them how reasonable the noble captains’ demands were, and what harm would follow from old Incredulity’s speech: how little reverence he had shown either to the captains or to their King, and how he had by implication charged them with unfaithfulness and treachery. “For what else,” they said, “can be made of his words, when he said he would not yield to their proposal, and added besides a supposition that the King would destroy us, when the King had sent us word before that he would show us mercy?” Then the crowd, now convinced of the harm old Incredulity had done, began to run together in groups everywhere, in every corner of the streets of Mansoul. First they began to mutter, then to talk openly, and after that they ran to and fro, crying as they ran, “Oh, the brave captains of Shaddai! If only we were under the government of the captains, and of Shaddai their King!” When the Lord Mayor heard that Mansoul was in an uproar, down he came to calm the people, thinking to quash their heat with the bulk and show of his presence. But when they saw him, they came running at him, and no doubt would have done him harm if he had not taken refuge in a house. Even so, they assaulted the house where he was with all their strength, meaning to pull it down around his ears; but the place was too strong, and they failed. So, taking some courage, he addressed the people from a window:
“Gentlemen, what is the reason for this uproar today?”

My Lord Understanding answered him. “It is because you and your master have not dealt rightly, as you should have, with the captains of Shaddai. You are at fault in three things. First, you would not let Mr. Conscience and me be present to hear your discussion. Second, you proposed terms of peace to the captains that could not possibly be granted, unless they meant their Shaddai to be a prince in title only, while Mansoul kept the power by law to live in all lewdness and vanity before him; and so, in effect, Diabolus would still be king here in power, and the other king only in name. Third, after the captains had shown us on what conditions they would receive us into mercy, you yourself undid it all again with your sour, ill-timed, and ungodly speech.”
When old Incredulity heard this, he cried out, “Treason! Treason! To arms! To arms, you trusty friends of Diabolus in Mansoul!”
“Sir,” said Understanding, “you may put whatever meaning you please on my words; but I am sure that the captains of so high a lord as theirs deserved better treatment at your hands.”

“That is little better,” said old Incredulity. “But sir, what I spoke, I spoke for my prince, for his government, and for the quieting of the people, whom you by your unlawful actions have today stirred up to mutiny against us.”

Then the old Recorder, whose name was Mr. Conscience, replied: “Sir, you ought not to throw back at my Lord Understanding what he has said. It is plain enough that he has spoken the truth, and that you are an enemy to Mansoul. Be convinced, then, of the evil of your insolent, impudent language, and of the grief you have caused the captains, yes, and of the damage you have done to Mansoul by it. Had you accepted the conditions, the sound of the trumpet and the alarm of war would by now have ceased around the town of Mansoul; but that dreadful sound goes on, and your lack of wisdom in your speech has been the cause of it.”

“Sir,” said old Incredulity, “if I live, I will carry your message to Diabolus, and there you shall have an answer to your words. Meanwhile we will seek the good of the town, and not ask your advice.”

“Sir,” said Understanding, “your prince and you are both foreigners to Mansoul, and not natives of it. And who can say that when you have brought us into greater straits, and see that you can save yourselves by no other means than flight, you will not leave us and shift for yourselves? Or set us on fire and go off in the smoke, or by the light of our burning, and so leave us in our ruins?”

“Sir,” said Incredulity, “you forget that you are under a governor, and that you ought to behave like a subject. And know this: when my lord the king hears of this day’s work, he will give you little thanks for your trouble.”

Now while these gentlemen were trading angry words, down from the walls and gates of the town came the Lord Willbewill, Mr. Prejudice, old Dwell-on-it, and several of the newly made aldermen and burgesses, and asked the reason for the commotion and uproar. At that every man began to tell his own tale, so that nothing could be heard clearly. Then silence was called for, and that old fox Incredulity began to speak. “My lord,” he said, “here are a couple of peevish gentlemen who, as the fruit of their bad dispositions, and, I fear, on the advice of one Mr. Discontent, have riotously gathered this company against me today, and have also tried to drive the town into acts of rebellion against our prince.”
Then all the Diabolonians present stood up and declared these things to be true.

Now when those who sided with my Lord Understanding and Mr. Conscience saw that they were likely to come off worst, because force and power lay on the other side, others came in to help and relieve them; so there was a great company on both sides. Then Incredulity’s side wanted the two old gentlemen hauled off to prison at once, but the other side said they should not. Then they began to cheer for their parties again. The Diabolonians cheered for old Incredulity, Forget-Good, the new aldermen, and their great one, Diabolus; and the other party cheered just as hard for Shaddai, the captains, his laws, and their mercifulness, and applauded their conditions and ways. So the quarrel went on a while, until at last they passed from words to blows, and now there were knocks on both sides. The good old gentleman Mr. Conscience was knocked down twice by one of the Diabolonians, whose name was Mr. Benumbing; and my Lord Understanding was nearly killed with an arquebus, an early handgun, except that the man who fired it did not aim straight. Nor did the other side escape entirely; for there was one Mr. Rashhead, a Diabolonian, who had his brains beaten out by Mr. Mind, the Lord Willbewill’s servant. And it made me laugh to see how old Mr. Prejudice was kicked and tumbled about in the dirt; for though not long before he had been made captain of a company of Diabolonians, to the hurt and damage of the town, now they had him under their feet, and I assure you he had his head cracked into the bargain by some of the Lord Understanding’s party. Captain Any-side, too, made himself a busy man in the brawl; but both sides were against him, because he was true to neither. Yet for his impudence he had one of his legs broken, and the man who did it wished it had been his neck. Much more harm was done on both sides, but this must not be forgotten: it was a wonder now to see how indifferent my Lord Willbewill was. He did not seem to take one side more than the other; only it was noticed that he smiled to see old Prejudice tumbled up and down in the dirt. And when Captain Any-side came limping up before him, he seemed to take very little notice of him.

Now when the uproar was over, Diabolus sent for my Lord Understanding and Mr. Conscience and threw them both into prison as the ringleaders and managers of this most grievous riot in Mansoul. So the town began to be quiet again. The prisoners were harshly used; indeed, Diabolus would have done away with them, except that the present moment did not serve for it, since there was war at all their gates.
